metadata.title: Social and emotional skills and young people's expectations of social status and mobility

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 public-use microdata for 15-year-old students in 27 countries, with analyses designed to reflect PISA’s complex sampling structure. For constructing country-specific ESCS decile cut-points and for mathematics achievement quintiles, the authors use PISA sampling weights to obtain nationally representative thresholds. In the regression/mediation estimation stage, they apply student final weights together with balanced replication weights (BRR) to compute standard errors that account for clustering and the complex survey design. The manuscript does not report a specific weight variable name (e.g., W_FSTUWT), but it explicitly states that both final weights and BRR replicate weights were used in all estimations.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the PISA 2022 public-use files for the subset of countries that administered (i) the expected relative social status by age 30 ladder item and (ii) the PISA 2022 social and emotional skills indicators. The analytic sample includes 205,231 15-year-old students in 27 countries. Missing data on key variables were handled via multiple imputation (10 imputed datasets) using chained equations, with the imputation model including all analysis variables plus auxiliary reading and science achievement scores; country fixed effects were included in the imputation model. The authors also report a robustness re-estimation excluding countries with the highest levels of missingness, with substantively similar conclusions.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 (15-year-olds) Expected relative social status by age 30 (social status ladder)
main_findings.target_variable: Expected relative social status (ERSS) at age 30 (1–10 ladder)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported as ML metrics (no predictive model reported); mediation/decomposition reported via path coefficients (β) and standard errors (SE).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 (15-year-olds) the study leveraged objective social status (ESCS), social and emotional skills (especially perseverance and assertiveness), and mathematics achievement quintiles to model expected relative social status at age 30, finding that ESCS is positively associated with ERSS and that perseverance (β≈0.210–0.213) and assertiveness (β≈0.221–0.222) show the strongest positive associations even after controls. This indicates that strengthening perseverance and assertiveness may help adolescents translate socioeconomic advantage into more ambitious (and potentially more motivating) future social-status expectations, though the evidence is correlational and not causal.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2022 microdata for 205,231 15-year-old students in 27 countries that administered both the expected relative social status ladder (by age 30) and the OECD social and emotional skills scales. The outcome is a 1–10 expected relative decile on a MacArthur-type social status ladder, while key predictors include ESCS-based objective social status deciles, seven social and emotional skills (perseverance, emotional control, stress resistance, empathy, cooperation, curiosity, assertiveness), and mathematics achievement quintiles derived from PISA mathematics plausible values. Missing data were addressed with multiple imputation via chained equations (10 datasets) and estimates were combined using Rubin’s rule; standard errors incorporate PISA complex sampling using final weights and BRR replicate weights. The paper reports path coefficients and mediation decompositions rather than ML predictive performance metrics, and it emphasizes that associations are correlational, so causal claims about mediation cannot be made.
data.null_fields_interpretation: Although the paper is included in a machine-learning search context, the analysis strategy is not ML-based: it reports multilevel variance decomposition and regression/mediation path coefficients with multiple imputation and survey-weighted standard errors, but it does not train or evaluate any supervised ML model. Consequently, ML technique fields are intentionally left empty and no PV-handling or missing-data transparency gaps are present (both are explicitly described).
